# Example
# Further Example

> When the clouds arrived, ten times the square root of a flock of swans flew to Lake Manasa, while one-eighth of the flock flew from the water's edge to a grove of land-lotuses. O girl, three pairs of swans were seen enjoying themselves in the water, which was lovely with young lotus stalks. Tell me the total number of the flock. (3)

**Prose order:** O girl! With the arrival of the clouds, ten times the square root of the flock of swans went to Lake Manasa. One-eighth of the flock flew from the water's edge to a land-lotus grove. And three pairs of swans were seen enjoying play in the water, adorned with young lotus stalks. If so, tell me the total number of the flock. (3)

**Meaning:** O beloved, who is sixteen years of age! There was a flock of swans. When the rainy season arrived, ten times the square root of them went to Lake Manasa, and one-eighth of the flock flew from the water's edge to the land-lotus grove. And three pairs <note>6 swans</note> of swans were seen playing with great affection in the water, which was beautiful with soft lotus stalks. Tell me, how many swans were in that flock? (3)

**Calculation:** The multiplier is 10. The fraction is 1/8. The visible amount is 6. Since the rule states "reduced by the fraction," here, by dividing the visible amount 6 by the remaining fraction 7/8, we obtain the visible amount 48/7. The multiplier becomes 80/7. Half of the multiplier is 40/7. Squaring this gives 1600/49. Adding this to the visible amount gives 1936/49. The square root of this is 44/7. Added to half the multiplier (40/7) and squared, the total number of swans is 144.

**Elaboration:** According to the rule mentioned in the second verse above, when one-eighth (1/8) is subtracted from one, it becomes 1/1 - 1/8 = 7/8. Dividing the visible amount of 6 by this, we get 6/1 ÷ 7/8 = 6/1 × 8/7 = 48/7. By adjusting the seven, 48/7 becomes the visible quantity. Similarly, dividing the multiplier 10 by 7/8, we get 10/1 ÷ 7/8 = 10/1 × 8/7 = 80/7. By adjusting the seven, 80/7 becomes the base quantity. Now, taking 48/7 as the visible quantity and 80/7 as the base, the operation is performed according to the method stated in the verse above. That is, half of the multiplier is 40/7. Squaring this gives 1600/49. This is added to the visible quantity 48/7...

Vasudeva is the supreme Brahman. His manifestation is the Supreme Person, who is unmanifest, devoid of qualities, peaceful, beyond the twenty-five elements, and immutable; that is, he is without change. 12

->The Lord, abiding within nature, is omnipresent, both external and internal.<-
->Sankarshana, at the beginning of creation, created the waters and deposited his energy within them. 13<-

Since it is impossible for the pure Brahman to be the direct cause of the world, [the author] explains: [the Lord] abiding within nature, or rather, associated with <term>Maya</term> <gloss>illusory power</gloss>, is omnipresent, both external and internal, as he is the material cause of the world. All these attributes should be understood as applying to Sankarshana, a portion of Vasudeva, by recognizing his identity with Vasudeva. Sankarshana, who is a portion of Vasudeva, first created the waters. In those waters, he deposited his energy, a specific power. 13

Experiential for all, the Lord Sankarshana entered into this nature and first created the waters. Afterward, he placed his own radiance, in the form of a seed, into those waters. 13

->That became a golden egg, covered everywhere by darkness.<-
->Therein, the eternal Aniruddha first manifested himself. 14<-

What happened thereafter? That water, combined with his energy, became a golden egg, spherical in shape, covered everywhere—both inside and outside—by darkness. The meaning is that a golden egg was produced in the space filled with darkness. There, in that golden egg, the eternal Lord Aniruddha, a portion of Vasudeva—and also a portion of Sankarshana—first manifested; he was not born, for the doctrine of <term>Satkaryavada</term> <gloss>the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause</gloss> is accepted. Just as oil exists in sesame seeds and is merely manifested, not created, so too was he manifested. 14

That radiance in the form of a seed took the shape of a golden egg. It was surrounded on all sides by darkness. There, within the egg, the eternal Lord Aniruddha first appeared. 14

->This Lord is described in the Vedas as Hiranyagarbha.<-
->He is called Aditya because he was the first to exist, and because he expands, he is called Surya. 15<-

Now, for the sake of public understanding, [the author] provides other names for him. This Lord Aniruddha, a portion of Sankarshana, who is endowed with the six qualities of majesty <note>original: <term>shadgunya-aishvarya</term></note>, is described or characterized in the Vedas as Hiranyagarbha because he resides within the golden egg as its core. The meaning is that he is famously known in the Vedas by the name Hiranyagarbha. Indeed, he is called <term>Aditya</term> <gloss>the First/Original</gloss> because he was the first to manifest. Because of his expansion—that is, because the world is manifested from him—he is called Surya.

"Hiranyagarbha existed in the beginning, the sole lord of all that is born." 

This is the scriptural text. 15

This very Lord is Hiranyagarbha, who is mentioned in the Vedas. In the beginning

<keywords>Surya Siddhanta, Vasudeva, Sankarshana, Hiranyagarbha, Aniruddha, nature, golden egg, Vedic scriptures</keywords>

A wise man, knowing his own limitations, should not proposition a woman who is suspicious, guarded, fearful, or supervised by her mother-in-law. (27)
Thus ends the second chapter, "The Means of Acquaintance and Solicitation," in the fifth book of the *Kamasutra* of Vatsyayana, dealing with the wives of others.

"Suspicious" means one who has become wary of the solicitor; "guarded" means one protected by sentries; "fearful" means one afraid of her husband; "supervised by her mother-in-law" means one living under the control of a mother-in-law. "Should not proposition" means one should not desire her, "knowing his own limitations," meaning one who has reached the certainty that he is incapable in this matter. (27)
Thus ends the forty-fourth section, "Solicitation."

Thus ends the second chapter, "The Means of Acquaintance and Solicitation," in the fifth book, dealing with the wives of others, of the *Jayamangala* commentary on the *Kamasutra* of Vatsyayana, composed by Yashodhara.

Chapter 3.

Even when solicitation has been attempted, there are women who are composed and bold whom one must examine. If their true feelings have not been revealed, then there is no special solicitation towards them. Therefore, the "Examination of Intent" is spoken of:
One who is soliciting should examine the behavior of the woman, for by that, her intent is examined. (1)

"Like a maiden," one should examine her "behavior," meaning her gestures. By this observation, her intent is examined. (1)

How is she to be won over? He says:
One who does not conceal her feelings should be won over by a female messenger. (2)

"One who does not conceal her feelings" means one who does not hide her amorous disposition. One should win her over through a messenger because of her boldness. (2)

One who rejects a solicitation but continues to associate with him, one should know her mind is divided; one should win her over gradually. (3)

"Rejecting a solicitation" made by the hero, but "continuing to associate" after waiting for some days, "meeting" with the hero again, one should know her "mind is divided," as she is worth examining, thinking "What should I do, I do not know." One should win her over gradually; one should not abandon her suddenly. (3)

He states a specific detail here:
If she, having rejected a solicitation, is seen again adorned with special ornaments, he should approach her in that same manner.

<summary>This page concludes the section on solicitation methods and begins the "Examination of Intent" (Bhavapariksha), detailing how a suitor should observe a woman's gestures and behavioral cues to determine if she is receptive or indecisive.</summary>
<keywords>Kamasutra, Vatsyayana, Yashodhara, Jayamangala, solicitation, female messengers, courtship, behavioral analysis</keywords>

it must be given. Its outcome is dependent upon him. Thus, you take it away. Hearing this, as soon as he awoke, he searched for the gold knot. Seeing it empty, he thought, "Oh, how has the wealth I earned with such difficulty vanished so easily? Having become penniless in vain, how shall I show my face to my wife or my friends?" Having decided this, he went back to Vardhamanapura. There, within a year, he earned five hundred gold coins and again started for his own home by a different path.

As the sun was setting, he reached the same banyan tree. "Alas, what misery. Why has this been started by one struck by fate? Once again, that same demon in the form of a banyan tree has arrived." While thinking this and pretending to be asleep, he saw those same two men on its branches. One of them said, "Doer, why did you give these five hundred gold coins to this Somilaka? Does your honor not know that apart from food and clothing, he has nothing more at all?" The other said, "Oh, worker, it must be given by me to those engaged in business. The result is dependent upon him. Why do you blame me?" Hearing this, as soon as Somilaka searched for the knot, he saw it empty. Then, filled with supreme detachment, he thought, "Alas, what is the point of my living without wealth? I shall hang myself on this banyan tree and give up my life."

Having decided this, he made a rope out of *darbha* grass <note>a sacred bunch grass used in ritual</note>, fastened a noose around his neck, approached a branch, and just as he was about to cast himself off after tying it, a man in the sky said this: "Oh Somilaka, do not commit such a rash act. I am that very wealth-taker who takes from you what is more than food and clothing."

<summary>Somilaka the weaver loses his hard-earned money twice to divine agents who claim his destiny only allows for basic sustenance; in despair, he attempts suicide, only to be addressed by the entity responsible for his misfortune.</summary>
<keywords>Panchatantra, Somilaka, weaver, wealth, destiny, suicide, banyan tree, supernatural intervention</keywords>

If war has indeed arrived, O King, why did you not prepare for it earlier? For, what kind of servant or minister is he who, without thought, advises a king to initiate the preparations for war and abandon his own position? Furthermore, one should always endeavor to conquer an enemy through means other than war, for when two parties are engaged in battle, the outcome is never certain. Moreover, one should attempt to overcome an enemy using conciliation, bribery, or dissension, either together or separately, but never by war. Additionally, every person is a hero as long as they have not yet encountered war; who would not be proud when the strength of the opponent remains unseen? Furthermore, a great result is not easily obtained by violent means when only minor measures are employed. However, having seen that war has arrived, one must treat the enemy with disregard. For,

<note>The Chakravaka bird, seeing the battle at hand, says: "O Great King, war should not be undertaken first. For, what kind of servant or minister is he who, without deliberation, advises a king to prepare for battle and abandon his own station? Moreover, one should strive to conquer an opponent through conciliation and other peaceful means, rather than through conflict, because when two sides are fighting, it is never certain who will emerge victorious. Additionally, one should attempt to resolve the matter with the enemy through conciliation, gifts, or sowing dissension, either individually or in combination, but never through war. Furthermore, everyone is a hero until they have actually fought, as no one knows the true strength of the other."</note>

<summary>This page discusses the folly of engaging in war, advising kings to prefer diplomacy, conciliation, and strategic maneuvering over military conflict due to the unpredictability of battle.</summary>
<keywords>Hitopadesha, War, Diplomacy, Politics, Strategy, Chakravaka, Conflict Resolution</keywords>

### Jiao Na

Scholar Kong, known as Xue Li, was a descendant of the Sage <note>a reference to Confucius</note>. He was a refined man, skilled in poetry. He had a close friend in Tiantai who sent him a letter of invitation, so Kong set out to meet him. Upon arriving, he found that his friend had passed away. Left stranded and unable to return home, he took up residence in Putuo Temple, where he worked as a scribe for the monks. 

About a hundred paces west of the temple stood the residence of Master Dan. The master was the descendant of a noble family, but due to a major lawsuit, his household had dwindled. He had moved to the countryside, leaving his town house vacant. 

One day, while heavy snow was falling and the paths were deserted, Kong happened to pass by the house. A youth came out, possessed of a remarkably elegant bearing. Seeing Kong, he hurried forward to greet him with courtesy, offering words of comfort and inviting him to step inside. Kong, feeling drawn to him, readily accepted. The house was not particularly large, but everywhere hung brocade curtains. On the walls were many paintings and scrolls by ancient masters, and on the desk lay a volume with a label reading *Langhuan Suo* <gloss>Trivial Records of the Langhuan Library</gloss>.

<summary>This passage introduces Scholar Kong, a refined man who becomes stranded at a temple and meets a mysterious, elegant youth at the vacant residence of Master Dan.</summary>
<keywords>Scholar Kong, Jiao Na, Putuo Temple, refinement, ancient scrolls, Langhuan Suo</keywords>

They all produced land and housing, but Cheng had already become the head of the household. His brothers were furious that he had curried favor <note>implying that Cheng gained the brothers' inheritance through deceit or manipulation</note> and went to his door to shame and harass him. Cheng, having lived among bandits for a long time, had grown accustomed to violence and intimidation. Upon hearing this, he was enraged and said, "I have returned with nowhere to live. I was fortunate that my third younger brother remembered our blood ties, and yet you condemn him? Do you wish to drive me away?" He threw stones at Xiao. Xiao, Ren, and Yi each took up staffs and beat Zhong and Xin countless times. 

Cheng did not wait for them to sue him; he sued them first. The magistrate summoned You-Yu to ask for his counsel. You-Yu, having no other choice, arrived, but he felt only shame. He hung his head and remained silent, shedding tears. When pressed for an answer, he requested only that the magistrate provide a fair judgment. The magistrate ruled that Xiao and the others must each contribute a portion of their land and property to Cheng, such that the division would be equal among the seven. From this point on, Ren and Yi grew to love and respect Cheng all the more.

While laughing and talking, the topic suddenly turned to the burial of their mother, and all of them wept. Cheng remarked, "To be so inhumane is to be no better than a beast." He then intended to open the grave to rebury her. Ren and Yi ran to inform You-Yu, who hurried back to remonstrate with him and stop him, but Cheng would not listen and set a date for the task.

<summary>Cheng, having adopted the aggressive habits of bandits, extorts land and property from his brothers through legal action and intimidation, while also demanding the exhumation and reburial of their mother.</summary>
<keywords>Cheng, family dispute, inheritance, legal judgment, reburial, filial piety</keywords>

they reversed the wooden sticks and beat him while he was standing. I do not know what implement they used, but they beat him until his face was cut in two places. We heard that the Mistress <note>referring to Aunt Xue</note> has a medicine for cudgel wounds here. Could you find a pill for me, Miss?"

Baochai heard this and hurriedly ordered Ying'er to find two pills to give to Ping'er. Baochai said, "Since that is the case, you go and convey my regards on my behalf; I shall not go myself." Ping'er promised Baochai and left. That is all for now.

Now, after Xiangling had met everyone and finished her evening meal, Baochai and the others went to visit their mother, so she went to the Xiaoxiang Pavilion. By this time, Daiyu was more than half recovered. Seeing that Xiangling had also moved into the garden to live, she was naturally pleased. Xiangling smiled and said, "Now that I have moved in, I will have some spare time. If you could teach me how to write poetry, it would be my great fortune!" Daiyu smiled and said, "If you want to learn to write poetry, you must take me as your teacher. Although I am not an expert, I can certainly manage to teach you." Xiangling laughed, "If that is truly the case, then I will take you as my teacher, but you must not get annoyed with me." Daiyu said, "What is so difficult about it that it is worth fretting over? It is nothing more than the <term>qi cheng zhuan he</term> <gloss>the four-part structure of a poem: introduction, development, transition, and conclusion</gloss>. The middle development and transition sections consist of two pairs of parallel couplets: level tones must be paired with oblique tones; abstract words with concrete ones, and vice versa. If you happen to produce a truly extraordinary line, it does not even matter if the tone patterns or the abstract and concrete are not perfectly matched."

Xiangling smiled and said, "No wonder that whenever I sneak a peek at a volume of old poetry, I find some lines that are perfectly parallel, while others are not. I also heard it said that, 'The first, third, and fifth characters do not matter, but the second, fourth, and sixth must be distinct.' Yet, when I look at the poems of the ancients, I see some that follow this, while in others, the second, fourth, and sixth characters are incorrect. This has puzzled me every day. Now that I hear you say this, it turns out these rules are not important at all; as long as the wording is novel and unusual, that is what matters most." Daiyu replied, "That is exactly the principle. The wording is ultimately a secondary matter; the primary importance lies in establishing the intent. If the sentiment is genuine, the words do not even need embellishment to be good. This is called 'not letting the words harm the intent.'"

Xiangling said, "I am fond of Lu Fangweng's lines: 'The heavy curtains remain unrolled, and the scent lingers long; the ancient inkstone is slightly concave, gathering much ink.' It sounds so vivid and interesting!" Daiyu responded, "Because you do not know poetry, you are attracted to such shallow and accessible things. Once you get trapped in that style, you will never be able to learn the proper way. Just listen to me: if you are truly serious about learning, I have the <term>Wang Mojie Quanji</term> <gloss>Complete Collection of Wang Wei</gloss> here. You should carefully study and memorize his one hundred five-syllable regulated verses first. After that, read one hundred and twenty of Old Du's <note>referring to Du Fu</note> seven-syllable regulated verses, and next, read one or two hundred of Li Qinglian's <note>referring to Li Bai</note> seven-syllable quatrains. Once you have built a foundation with these three men, then take a look at the works of Tao Yuanming, Ying, Liu, Xie, Ruan, Yu, and Bao. Since you are such a clever and quick-witted person, you will be a poet yourself within a year!" Xiangling heard this and laughed, "If that is the case, good sister, please bring those books out for me so I can take them back; reading a few poems at night would be wonderful." Upon hearing this, Daiyu ordered Zijian to bring Wang Youcheng's <note>another name for Wang Wei</note> five-syllable regulated verses and handed them to Xiangling, saying, "Only look at the ones with red circles; those are my selections. Read them one by one. If you don't understand something, ask your sister <note>Baochai</note>, or if you happen to run into me, I will explain it to you."

Xiangling took the poems and returned to the Hengwu Courtyard. Setting aside all other matters, she sat under the lamp and began to read them one by one. Baochai urged her to go to sleep several times, but she would not. Seeing her such diligence, Baochai had no choice but to let her be.

One day, just after Daiyu had finished washing and dressing, she saw Xiangling bringing the book over, humming and wanting to exchange it for Du's regulated verses. Daiyu smiled and asked, "How many have you managed to memorize in total?" Xiangling smiled and said, "I have read all the ones with red circles." Daiyu asked, "Have you gained any understanding from them?" Xiangling smiled and said, "I have gained some understanding, but I am not sure if it is correct. Let me recite some for you to hear."

<summary>Daiyu instructs Xiangling on the study of classical poetry, emphasizing the importance of intent over rigid structural rules and recommending the works of Wang Wei, Du Fu, and Li Bai.</summary>
<keywords>Daiyu, Xiangling, Poetry, Wang Wei, Du Fu, Li Bai, literary instruction</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: Li Ru urged Dong Zhuo to appoint famous scholars to win public favor. Dong followed this advice and recommended Cai Yong for his talent. Dong ordered him to report for duty.</meta>

Cai Yong refused at first. Dong Zhuo was furious and sent a messenger to tell Cai, "If you do not come, I will exterminate your clan." Fearing for his life, Cai Yong had no choice but to obey the order and arrive. Dong Zhuo was overjoyed to see him and promoted him three times in one month, eventually appointing him as a Palace Attendant, treating him with great closeness and favor. <gloss>Always relying on the patronage of the powerful as Wang Feng and Yang Xiong did. Fearing one's own body might end up as firewood, or buried by a woodcutter on Mount Kun.</gloss>

Meanwhile, the Young Emperor, Empress Dowager He, and Lady Tang were trapped in the Yong'an Palace. Their clothing and food were gradually running low, and the Young Emperor’s tears never dried. <gloss>As the later king said, the days and months spent here are difficult.</gloss> One day, he happened to see a pair of swallows flying in the courtyard and recited a poem. <gloss>In the empty courtyard, birds fly and dance; in this cold palace and abandoned temple, I am alone, and my years are my own.</gloss>

The poem went:

Tender grass, green and dense with mist,
The pair of swallows fly with grace.
The Luo River, a single ribbon of blue,
People on the road admire its charm.
<gloss>The first half of the poem sings of the swallows and gazes into the distance.</gloss>
Deep within the blue clouds lies the palace where I once lived.
<gloss>Gazing until the eyes ache at the old palace, unable to fly there; truly, I am not as fortunate as the pair of swallows that can return to their old nest. How tragic.</gloss>
Who will act with loyalty and righteousness,
And vent the resentment in my heart?
<gloss>The second half is a poem of personal desire. The poem is well-written.</gloss>

Dong Zhuo often sent people to spy on them. That day, his agents intercepted this poem and presented it to him. Dong Zhuo said, "He is full of resentment and writes poetry. There is sufficient cause to kill him." <gloss>There is a famous precedent for killing him to teach the world a lesson.</gloss> He then ordered Li Ru to lead eighteen armed guards into the palace to murder the Emperor. The Emperor, the Empress Dowager, and Lady Tang were sitting on the upper floor when a palace maid reported that Li Ru had arrived. The Emperor was terrified. Li Ru presented a cup of poisoned wine to the Emperor. <gloss>It is ironic that this poem, which mentions drinking, would meet its end through this very act of drinking, which is usually a refined affair.</gloss>

<summary>Li Ru pressures the scholar Cai Yong into serving Dong Zhuo, while the imprisoned Young Emperor expresses his despair through poetry, leading Dong Zhuo to order his assassination via poison.</summary>
<keywords>Li Ru, Dong Zhuo, Cai Yong, Young Emperor, Empress Dowager He, Lady Tang, assassination, regicide, poisoned wine</keywords>

### The Nineteenth Chapter 19.

Now we shall explain the chapter on the care of the wounded <term>Vraṇitopāsanīya</term>.

Here we commence the explanation of the chapter on the conduct regarding wounds.

The physician should first look for a dwelling for the wounded person, and that dwelling should be constructed in a place with a favorable environment. 1. In a house with a favorable environment, which is clean and free from wind and sunlight, and sheltered from drafts, there will be no physical, accidental, or mental diseases. 2. He should prepare a spacious, well-spread, and pleasant bed with the head toward the east, provided with weapons <note>traditionally for protection against malevolent spirits</note>. 3. The wounded person will have ease of movement on a well-spread bed. The gods dwell in the eastern direction, therefore one should not have the head oriented toward that direction. 4.

When soaked lentils, clean and sweet, are combined with cool fruits and prepared in a rich buffalo meat broth seasoned with yogurt and pomegranate, and further enriched with flour, coriander, cumin, and dry ginger, this soup when consumed with a meal prevents the depletion of vital essence <term>śukra</term> <gloss>semen/vital reproductive fluid</gloss>. (8)
> This is the buffalo meat broth for virility.

One who consumes fresh fish or fried small <term>śapharī</term> <gloss>a type of small fish</gloss> cooked in hot clarified butter <term>ghṛta</term> <gloss>ghee</gloss> will not experience exhaustion during sexual activity. (9)
> These are the fish sautéed in ghee for virility.

One seeking to conceive a child should consume <term>rohita</term> <gloss>a species of carp</gloss> fish fried in ghee and cooked in goat meat broth, followed by drinking the remaining broth. (10)
> This is the preparation for conception.

Prepare cakes by mixing minced fish meat with asafoetida, rock salt, and coriander, adding wheat flour, and frying them in ghee. Alternatively, cook fatty, sour, and salty fish in buffalo meat broth. Once the liquid has reduced, crush the fish, add black pepper, cumin, coriander, a small amount of asafoetida, and fresh ghee. Use this as a filling for the lentil cakes. These two preparations of cakes increase virility, enhance strength, promote joy and attractiveness, provide nourishment, and are supreme promoters of vital essence. (11)
> These are the two cake preparations for virility.
